title: Cohere Pricing 2026 for Trial, Production and Enterprise
summary: Cohere pricing has Trial and Production tiers. Start with Trial, upgrade to Production when real users arrive, or contact sales for special features.
body_markdown:
## Hidden costs and limits Cohere users hit


Beyond overlap, three things add cost the price page never shows: trial throttling, per-search rerank billing and re-embedding after a model change.


### Trial key limits and commercial-use rules


Put a paying user on a trial key and you are breaking the terms, since the keys are free but meant for non-commercial use. The throttling shows the same intent. According to[Cohere's rate-limit docs](https://docs.cohere.com/docs/rate-limits) :


- Chat on Command A allows 20 calls per minute on a trial key against 500 on production
- Rerank goes from 10 to 1,000 calls per minute
- Image embedding goes from 5 to 400 calls per minute


Loop a prototype over a few hundred documents and it will stall at the trial ceiling; the Rerank ceiling of 10 is the first one you'll hit.


### Cohere Rerank and Embed billing surprises


Because rerank is billed per search unit, and one unit covers a query against up to 100 documents, sending 150 candidates costs two units, so trimming candidate lists to 100 halves that line.


Retrieval then inflates the chat bill, because every chunk you pass to Command becomes input tokens, and output tokens cost more per token than input.


Pass fewer, better-ranked chunks and the Command input shrinks; that's the real return on paying for Rerank.


### Cohere re-embedding and index maintenance costs


Change embedding models and you re-embed the whole corpus, because vectors from different models aren't interchangeable. At 10 million chunks, a model swap is a full second indexing bill, plus the overlap duplication from the previous section.


Pin the model version, store it with each vector, and treat a switch as a budgeted migration.


### Enable batching and automatic retries


For the dull parts of this bill, Activepieces suits well. It is an MIT-licensed core with 746 integrations, a count taken from the community integrations directory in its open source GitHub monorepo, and you reach Cohere through its Cohere integration or a plain HTTP step.


A scheduled flow can embed new documents in off-hours batches, so you stop re-sending unchanged text. A retry step with backoff handles 429 responses when you hit the limits above, instead of dropping the request.


Add a logging step that writes token counts and search units to a sheet or database, and you get a cost-per-run figure you can check against the invoice.


Activepieces' published pricing page lists 1 credit per flow run, whatever the number of steps, whereas Zapier's pricing page bills per task and Make's per module, so the embed, retry and logging steps cost the same as a flow with one.
